west-highlands-skye.title: The West Highlands and Skye
story: This is the Scotland most people picture: mountains running down into sea lochs, single-track roads, islands on the horizon. It is also the country of the Jacobites, and their story runs along the route day by day.

The journey passes Glencoe, where a massacre in 1692 is still remembered, and Glenfinnan, where Bonnie Prince Charlie raised his standard in 1745. It crosses to Skye, where Flora MacDonald later helped him escape, and comes back east to the moor at Culloden, where it ended. Five days, taken at a pace that lets you feel the place.

days.title: North to Glencoe
highlights: Collected and driven north as the landscape opens out
Rannoch Moor, then the descent into Glencoe
A Highland estate for the night
days.onTheRoad: The figure of 38 dead at Glencoe comes from the soldiers who did the killing. Modern research puts it nearer 30.

days.title: The Road to the Isles and over to Skye
highlights: Fort William, then west on the Road to the Isles
Glenfinnan and its viaduct
Across to Skye beneath Eilean Donan
days.onTheRoad: Eilean Donan looks medieval, but the Navy blew it up in 1719 with 343 barrels of captured gunpowder. What stands today was rebuilt and finished in 1932.

days.title: Skye
highlights: The Trotternish ridge and the Quiraing with a guide who knows the island
A tasting at a distillery, arranged in your own time rather than the crowd's
An evening at a country house on the shore
days.onTheRoad: The MacLeods' Fairy Flag is said to come from the fairies. A V&A expert found the silk was woven in Syria or Rhodes.

days.title: Loch Ness and Inverness
highlights: Back over the bridge and east through Glen Shiel
Along Loch Ness, with a stop at Urquhart Castle
A country house near Inverness for the night
days.onTheRoad: Urquhart Castle was not blown up by government troops. In 1690 its own garrison blew up the gatehouse so the Jacobites could not use it.

days.title: Culloden and Speyside
highlights: The moor at Culloden, early, before the visitors
Into Speyside, and a distillery that opens its doors for you
A castle for the night, and a dinner to match the setting
days.onTheRoad: Within a lifetime of Culloden it was illegal for a Highlander to wear tartan. A second offence meant seven years' transportation.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Driven to Inverness Airport for your flight

edinburgh-heart-of-scotland.title: Edinburgh and the Heart of Scotland
story: Three days is enough to understand why Scotland's story is told the way it is. It begins in a capital built in two halves: the medieval Old Town, all closes and wynds on its ridge, and the Georgian New Town laid out below it by a 26-year-old architect who won the competition in 1766.

From there the road runs north to Stirling, the hinge of the country's history. Wallace fought below its castle in 1297, and Bruce won at Bannockburn in sight of it in 1314. Then it turns west into the Trossachs and down to Loch Lomond, Rob Roy's country, which Walter Scott's novel made famous in 1817. The last two nights are spent out among the lochs and hills.

days.title: Edinburgh
highlights: Met at the airport and settled into the heart of the Old Town
An afternoon in the closes and wynds with a guide who knows the stories the crowds walk past
An evening at the castle, then dinner at one of the city's finest tables
days.onTheRoad: In 1828 Burke and Hare murdered sixteen people within a short walk of here and sold them to an anatomist. Their crimes gave the language the word "burking".

days.title: Stirling and into the Trossachs
highlights: Stirling Castle, where Mary, Queen of Scots was crowned in 1543, and the field of Bannockburn below it
Doune Castle on the road west
A country house in the Trossachs for the next two nights
days.onTheRoad: The Scots at Bannockburn were outnumbered perhaps two or three to one. On the first day Bruce killed an English knight in single combat with an axe.

days.title: Loch Lomond
highlights: A morning on Loch Lomond in a private boat
Lunch by the water at Luss
Back through the Trossachs for a last evening at the house
days.onTheRoad: Rob Roy is buried a short drive north at Balquhidder. His stone reads "MacGregor Despite Them", a defiance of the law that outlawed his very name.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Driven to Glasgow or Edinburgh Airport for your flight

grand-sweep.title: The Grand Sweep, South to Far North
story: A week from the capital to the empty roads of the far north is the journey people take once and remember for good. It follows roads first built by soldiers: General Wade laid some 240 miles of military road after the 1715 rising to hold the Highlands down. Today the same country is the most open space in Britain.

It passes through the history that shaped the north. The Jacobites rose and fell here, and within a lifetime of Culloden came the Clearances, which emptied whole glens. Then, in Speyside, it ends with a happier story: the whisky smugglers who went legal.

days.title: Edinburgh
highlights: The Old Town with a private guide
The castle
A dinner to set the tone for the week

days.title: Stirling, Glencoe and the Highlands
highlights: North through Stirling
Rannoch Moor and Glencoe
A private estate for the night, and the first real sense of the scale of the place
days.onTheRoad: General Wade's road-builders worked for twelve years. A stone is said to carry the couplet "If you had seen this road before it was made".

days.title: Skye
highlights: Over to Skye beneath Eilean Donan
Its ridges and pools
A tasting, and a night on the island

days.title: Torridon and the North West
highlights: The great coastal road north through Torridon towards Ullapool
Mountains on one side and the sea on the other
The best room on the route waiting at the end of the drive
days.onTheRoad: The North Coast 500 was only named as a route in 2015, but these roads are centuries older, and many are still single track.

days.title: The North Coast
highlights: North through Assynt to the empty beaches of the north coast
Dunnet Head, the true northern tip of the mainland
A night by the sea
days.onTheRoad: John o' Groats is famous for being the end of the road, but it is not the northern tip of mainland Britain. That is Dunnet Head, further west along this coast.

days.title: Sutherland and south to Speyside
highlights: Dunrobin Castle and the story of the Clearances, told from both sides
Over the Dornoch Firth and south into Speyside
A castle for the last two nights
days.onTheRoad: The last woman executed for witchcraft in Britain was burned at Dornoch in the 1720s. "Janet Horne" was a name used for any witch, so her real name may be lost.

days.title: Speyside
highlights: Whisky done properly: private tastings and a cask or two off the usual path
A castle dinner to close the week
days.onTheRoad: The Excise Act of 1823 made it worth going legal. Licensed whisky almost doubled in a single year, and George Smith of Glenlivet was first in line for a licence.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Driven to Inverness or Aberdeen Airport for your flight

golf-east-coast.title: A Week on the Links, Fife to Royal Deeside
story: The first written record of golf in Scotland is the moment it was banned. In 1457 Parliament ordered that golf be "utterly cried down", because men should be practising archery. They took no notice. Three centuries later St Andrews cut its course to eighteen holes, and the rest of the world followed.
This week follows the game up the east coast, from the town that set its rules to some of the oldest and most testing links in the world, with a day away from the course in Royal Deeside to finish.

days.title: Arrival in Fife
highlights: Met at the airport and driven to a private house near St Andrews
Dinner from the house chef, and a briefing on the week

days.title: St Andrews
highlights: The R&A World Golf Museum
A round on the Castle Course, on the cliffs above the North Sea
Dinner in the town
days.onTheRoad: In 1764 St Andrews cut its round from 22 holes to 18, and that is why a round of golf is 18 holes today.

days.title: Carnoustie
highlights: A talk on the course and its championship history
A round on Carnoustie Golf Links, one of the toughest tests of links golf anywhere
days.onTheRoad: On the Tay crossing you can see the stumps of the first Tay Bridge, which fell in a storm in 1879 and took a train with it.

days.title: North to Aberdeenshire
highlights: The clifftop ruin of Dunnottar Castle
An afternoon round at Cruden Bay
A private house in Aberdeenshire and an evening whisky tasting
days.onTheRoad: Bram Stoker holidayed at Cruden Bay and wrote early chapters of Dracula there. The ruined castle nearby may have inspired him.

days.title: Royal Aberdeen
highlights: The Granite City, and lunch by the harbour
An afternoon at Royal Aberdeen, one of the oldest golf clubs in the world
days.onTheRoad: Aberdeen's grey granite sparkles because of the mica in it, which is why it is called the Silver City by the Sea.

days.title: Royal Deeside
highlights: A day away from the course in the country Queen Victoria fell for in 1848
In early September, the Braemar Gathering
days.onTheRoad: At a Highland games the caber is scored on how straight it lands, like the hand of a clock at twelve, not on how far it goes.

days.title: Back to Edinburgh
highlights: South through Angus and over the Tay
A final afternoon and night in the city
Dinner to close the week

days.title: Departure
highlights: Driven to Edinburgh Airport for your flight

corporate-highlands.title: A Programme in the Highlands
story: The best incentive trips are remembered for the moments the group shared, not for the agenda. This programme brings a team from the capital into the Highlands and gives them a castle of their own for four nights.

The days are built around experiences that pull a group together: a challenge on a Highland estate, an evening ceilidh, and whisky at its source. There is plenty of time for the scenery to do its work, too.

days.title: Edinburgh
highlights: The group is met at the airport and taken to a landmark hotel
An evening walk through the darker side of the Old Town
Dinner together

days.title: Stirling, Loch Lomond and north
highlights: A private visit to Stirling Castle
Lunch aboard on Loch Lomond
North to a private castle for four nights, with a gala dinner on the first evening

days.title: Glencoe
highlights: A challenge on a Highland estate: clay shooting, off-road driving, and events in the spirit of the Highland games
A ceilidh at the castle in the evening, which tends to be the night everyone remembers
days.onTheRoad: A ceilidh was originally not a dance at all but a visit: neighbours gathering on winter nights to tell stories and sing.

days.title: Lochaber
highlights: A private distillery tour and tasting
An afternoon to walk, fish or simply take in the surroundings
Dinner at the castle

days.title: The Road to the Isles
highlights: The steam train over the Glenfinnan Viaduct, from June to October
A Land Rover safari into the hills for those who would rather stay on the ground
A farewell dinner, and a piper to close the trip
days.onTheRoad: Bonnie Prince Charlie raised his standard at Glenfinnan in 1745. The monument by the loch marks the start of the rising that ended at Culloden.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Transfers to Glasgow Airport, with the option to stay on

abbeys-and-border-country.title: Abbeys and Border Country
story: The Borders are a short drive from Edinburgh and a different country. For centuries this was the frontier, burned by English armies and raided by reiving families, and the great abbeys David I founded in the twelfth century were wrecked and rebuilt more than once.

Three days is enough to follow that story from Rosslyn Chapel to the Tweed. Sir Walter Scott fell for this valley and turned a farm into a fantasy of a house, and the quiet roads between the abbeys, the houses and the river are made for taking slowly.

days.title: Rosslyn and the Tweed valley
highlights: Rosslyn Chapel, founded by William Sinclair in the 1450s
Peebles, and a first look at the Tweed
Traquair House, where brewing goes back to 1739 (March to November)
days.onTheRoad: The Bear Gates at Traquair have been shut for over two centuries. Legend says they will not reopen until a Stuart king returns. The record suggests they were closed in 1796, after a countess died.

days.title: Abbeys and Walter Scott
highlights: Abbotsford, the house Sir Walter Scott built on a farm nicknamed Clarty Hole
Melrose Abbey, where the heart of Robert the Bruce lies
Dryburgh Abbey, and Scott's grave
days.onTheRoad: The heart of Robert the Bruce lies at Melrose. A lead casket found under the Chapter House was reburied there in 1998.

days.title: Jedburgh, Mellerstain and Kelso
highlights: Jedburgh Abbey, where Alexander III married in 1285
Mellerstain House and its Robert Adam library (April to September)
Floors Castle at Kelso, beside the Tweed, then back to Edinburgh for the last night
days.onTheRoad: Alexander III married Yolande de Dreux at Jedburgh in October 1285. His death the following year plunged Scotland into the crisis that led to the Wars of Independence.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Hand back the car at Edinburgh Airport for your flight

perthshire-and-angus.title: Perthshire and Angus
story: Perthshire is where Scotland crowned its kings, where the Jacobites won at Killiecrankie in 1689, and where Victorian visitors came for the scenery once Queen Victoria had praised it in 1842.
Four days lets you take it in order: Scone and the river at Dunkeld, the pass and Blair Castle, Wade's bridge at Aberfeldy and an ancient yew, then east to Glamis and the V&A in Dundee.

days.title: Scone and Dunkeld
highlights: Scone Palace and Moot Hill, where the Kings of Scots were crowned (April to October)
Along the Tay to Dunkeld and Birnam
An afternoon by the river, and a country house near Dunkeld for the night
days.onTheRoad: On Moot Hill the Kings of Scots were inaugurated on the Stone of Destiny. Robert the Bruce was crowned at Scone in 1306, and the last coronation here was Charles II's in 1651.

days.title: Pitlochry, Killiecrankie and Blair Castle
highlights: The dam at Pitlochry and its salmon ladder
The pass at Killiecrankie, where the Jacobites charged in 1689
Blair Castle, the last castle in the British Isles to be besieged (April to October)
days.onTheRoad: At Killiecrankie on 27 July 1689 the Jacobite Highlanders fired one volley, threw down their muskets and charged. The government army broke in minutes, but their leader, Viscount Dundee, was fatally wounded.

days.title: Aberfeldy, Fortingall and Drummond
highlights: Wade's Bridge at Aberfeldy
The Fortingall Yew, which may be anything from 1,500 to 9,000 years old
Drummond Castle Gardens, laid out as a giant saltire (May to October)
days.onTheRoad: In 1769 the trunk of the Fortingall Yew measured 52 feet round, before souvenir hunters cut pieces off to make drinking cups.

days.title: Glamis and Dundee
highlights: Glamis Castle, where Princess Margaret was born in 1930 (April to October)
V&A Dundee, and Mackintosh's Oak Room
Across the Tay and south to Edinburgh for the last night
days.onTheRoad: Look upstream of the rail bridge at Dundee and you can see the stumps of the first Tay Bridge, which fell in a storm in December 1879 and took a train with it.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Hand back the car at Edinburgh Airport for your flight

oban-argyll-and-kintyre.title: Oban, Argyll and Kintyre
story: Argyll is where the first kingdom of the Scots began, and the road through it runs past the evidence: standing stones and a carved footprint at Kilmartin, a Campbell castle on Loch Fyne, a MacDougall stronghold at Oban and a canal built to save sailors the long way round the Mull of Kintyre.

Five days takes in all of it, from Loch Lomond to the far end of the Kintyre peninsula, with the sea beside you for most of the way. At the end of the road, Campbeltown once had more than thirty distilleries and the links run along the shore.

days.title: Loch Lomond to Inveraray
highlights: Along the shore of Loch Lomond
Oysters and a view at the head of Loch Fyne
Inveraray Castle, seat of the Duke of Argyll (March to October)
days.onTheRoad: Inveraray is the seat of the Duke of Argyll, chief of Clan Campbell. Its Armoury Hall has the highest ceiling in Scotland.

days.title: Inveraray to Oban
highlights: Loch Awe, and Ben Cruachan above it
Dunstaffnage Castle, on the way into Oban
An evening at the harbour, and a climb to McCaig's Tower
days.onTheRoad: Dunstaffnage was built by the MacDougalls in the 1220s and taken by Robert the Bruce in 1308. In 1746 it briefly held Flora MacDonald, after she helped Bonnie Prince Charlie escape.

days.title: Oban and the Appin coast
highlights: Ardchattan Priory and its gardens, across Loch Etive (April to October)
Castle Stalker, on its rock in the loch
An afternoon boat trip from Oban to look for wildlife
days.onTheRoad: McCaig's Tower above Oban is a banker's attempt at a Roman Colosseum. It was built to give local stonemasons work in hard times, and never finished because McCaig died in 1902.

days.title: Kilmartin Glen and down to Kintyre
highlights: Kilmartin Glen, with more than 800 ancient monuments within six miles
Dunadd, where the first kings of the Scots are thought to have been made
The Crinan Canal, then the long road down the Kintyre peninsula to Campbeltown
days.onTheRoad: The Crinan Canal is nine miles long with fifteen locks. It lets boats skip the passage round the Mull of Kintyre, and Queen Victoria came through in 1847 in a boat towed by four horses.

days.title: Campbeltown and Machrihanish
highlights: A round at Machrihanish Golf Club or Machrihanish Dunes, or at Dunaverty at the southern tip
A distillery tour in Campbeltown
The last evening in a town that once called itself the whisky capital of the world
days.onTheRoad: At its height Campbeltown had more than thirty distilleries. Three survive.

days.title: Departure
highlights: An early start, and the car handed back at Glasgow Airport for your flight

ayrshire-and-the-south-west.title: Ayrshire and the South West
story: Ayrshire is Robert Burns country and the birthplace of championship golf, and the road south runs past both. Prestwick held the first Open in 1860, Royal Troon and Turnberry are a short drive down the coast, and the cottage where Burns was born still stands at Alloway.

Beyond lies Dumfries and Galloway, quieter again: a triangular castle on the Solway, a pink palace in the hills and a links with the water at its edge. Six days gives the golfers their rounds and the rest of the party the castles, and ends in Glasgow.

days.title: Kelburn and the Ayrshire coast
highlights: Kelburn Castle, its walls covered in graffiti by Brazilian artists
The coast road south to Troon
A first evening by the sea
days.onTheRoad: In 2007 Lord Glasgow invited Brazilian graffiti artists to paint the castle walls. It was meant to be temporary, but in 2011 he asked to keep it.

days.title: Prestwick and Alloway
highlights: A round at Prestwick Golf Club, where the first Open was played
The Robert Burns Birthplace Museum at Alloway
An evening in Ayr
days.onTheRoad: The first Open was played at Prestwick in October 1860 by eight professionals, for a red leather belt. You can still play the Alps and the Cardinal, holes from that first championship.

days.title: Culzean and Turnberry
highlights: Culzean Castle and its country park (March to November)
The Turnberry coast, and a round at Turnberry for those who play
Dinner back along the coast
days.onTheRoad: When the Kennedys gave Culzean to the nation in 1945, they insisted the top-floor flat go to General Eisenhower. He stayed four times, once as President.

days.title: Dumfries House and into Galloway
highlights: Dumfries House, saved for the nation in 2007
On across the hills to Dumfries
A country house near Dumfries for the next two nights
days.onTheRoad: In 2007 the then Prince of Wales led a consortium that raised about £45 million to save Dumfries House and its original Chippendale furniture from being sold off.

days.title: Caerlaverock and the Solway
highlights: Caerlaverock Castle, the only triangular castle in Britain
A round at Southerness Golf Club, beside the Solway
Back to Dumfries for the evening
days.onTheRoad: Edward I besieged Caerlaverock in 1300, and the siege was written up as a heraldic poem.

days.title: Drumlanrig and Glasgow
highlights: Drumlanrig Castle, the Pink Palace in the hills above the Nith (February to October)
North to Glasgow
The Burrell Collection in Pollok Park, and a last evening in the city
days.onTheRoad: Sir William Burrell gave Glasgow his collection in 1944 on condition that it was housed at least sixteen miles from the city centre. It took nearly forty years, and the gift of Pollok Park, to open the museum in 1983.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Hand back the car at Glasgow Airport for your flight

north-coast-slowly.title: The North Coast, Taken Slowly
story: The North Coast 500 was named as a route only in 2015, but the roads are far older, and the history along them is the Highlands' hardest: Culloden, the Clearances and the castles that outlasted both.
Seven days is enough to take it slowly, with a castle or a garden to break each drive, single-track roads for the empty stretches and the sea in sight for most of the way.

days.title: Cawdor, Fort George and Culloden
highlights: Cawdor Castle, built some four hundred years after Macbeth died (April to October)
Fort George, a working barracks that was never attacked
The moor at Culloden, and Inverness for the night
days.onTheRoad: The battle at Culloden was over in less than an hour. The clan headstones you see were put up in 1881, more than a century later.

days.title: Dornoch and Dunrobin
highlights: Dornoch, where golf has been played since at least 1616
Dunrobin Castle, the largest house in the northern Highlands (April to October)
The coast road north to Wick
days.onTheRoad: Golf has been played at Dornoch since at least 1616. The Dornoch boy Donald Ross went on to become one of America's great course designers.

days.title: John o' Groats and the Castle of Mey
highlights: John o' Groats and the Pentland Firth
The Castle of Mey, the Queen Mother's home (May to September)
Dunnet Head, the true northern tip of mainland Britain
days.onTheRoad: The Queen Mother found Mey half-derelict the year after the King died, bought it, and came every August and October for nearly fifty years.

days.title: The north coast to Assynt
highlights: The north coast road to Tongue, with empty beaches on the way
Durness, in the far north-west corner
Over the Kylesku bridge into Assynt
days.onTheRoad: The North Coast 500 was launched in March 2015 as a 516-mile loop from Inverness Castle. The roads are older than the name, and many are single-track, so there is no prize for hurrying.

days.title: Ullapool to Torridon
highlights: Ullapool and its harbour
Inverewe Garden, where redwoods and rhododendrons grow at the latitude of Moscow
The road round to Torridon, with the mountains above
days.onTheRoad: Inverewe stands at the same latitude as Moscow. Thanks to the Gulf Stream and a twenty-year-old's vision in 1862, redwoods and rhododendrons grow there.

days.title: Torridon to Kintail
highlights: The road along Loch Torridon and Loch Carron
Eilean Donan Castle, with time to spare (February to December)
An afternoon at your own pace on the shore of Loch Duich
days.onTheRoad: In 1719 forty-six Spanish soldiers held Eilean Donan for the Jacobites. When the Navy took it they found 343 barrels of gunpowder and used every one to blow it up, so what you see is a 20th-century rebuild.

days.title: Glen Shiel, Loch Ness and Inverness
highlights: Through Glen Shiel and the Great Glen to Fort Augustus
Urquhart Castle above Loch Ness
A last evening in Inverness
days.onTheRoad: The most famous Nessie photograph, the 1934 "surgeon's photograph", was a toy submarine with a putty head. When scientists sampled the loch's DNA in 2018 they found no reptiles, but a great many eels.

days.title: Departure
highlights: Hand back the car at Inverness Airport for your flight
